This section explains the major implementation tools used in the system.
4.3.1 Python and Flask

Python was used for the backend implementation because it provides a clear and flexible environment for building web services and managing application logic. Flask was used as the backend web framework. The Flask backend handled the core voting operations, including mock NIN accreditation, login, session validation, camera-verification status, event retrieval, vote submission, proof verification, public board records, tally computation, and admin operations. The backend also acted as the security control point because it enforced voter eligibility, event status, vote-value validation, duplicate-vote prevention, and proof verification before ballot storage. This ensured that the system did not rely on frontend checks alone.

The backend exposed several application programming interface endpoints to support the voting workflow. These included endpoints for registration, login, camera-based verification, vote submission, proof verification, public board retrieval, tally retrieval, event retrieval, health checking, proof-engine health checking, and admin registry operations. The vote submission endpoint was especially important because it controlled whether a ballot would be accepted. A ballot was stored only after the backend confirmed the voter session, checked the event, validated the vote value, checked duplicate-vote status, generated a proof, verified the proof, encrypted the ballot, computed the proof hash, and stored the accepted ballot record.
4.3.2 React

React was used to implement the frontend of the prototype. The frontend provided the screens and workflows needed by voters and administrators. For voters, the interface supported landing-page access, mock NIN accreditation, camera-based prototype verification, event selection, binary ballot selection, vote review, ballot submission, receipt display, public verification-board access, and tally viewing. For administrators, the interface supported mock voter registry management and prototype reset operations. The frontend was designed to guide users through the voting process in a clear sequence so that they would understand when they were being accredited, verified, allowed to vote, and given a receipt.

The React frontend did not independently decide whether a voter was eligible or whether a ballot was valid. Instead, it sent requests to the Flask backend and displayed the backend response. This design was necessary because client-side validation can be bypassed by a malicious user. The frontend therefore served mainly as the presentation and interaction layer, while the backend enforced the voting rules. The frontend was also configured to communicate with the deployed backend through an environment variable, allowing the hosted Vercel frontend to connect to the Railway backend.

Winterfell was used as the zk-STARK proof engine for the prototype. The proof engine was responsible for generating and verifying proof artifacts connected to the ballot acceptance process. The system used Winterfell after an earlier exploration of Cairo was discontinued due to an upstream verification issue that affected the proof workflow. Winterfell was selected for the final implementation because it successfully supported proof generation and verification for the controlled binary ballot scenario. The implemented proof engine generated and verified proofs for valid Yes and No ballot values.

The proof engine was integrated into the backend voting workflow. When a voter submitted a ballot, the backend checked the normal voting conditions and then invoked the proof engine. The generated proof was verified before the encrypted ballot record was stored. If proof verification failed, the ballot was not accepted. After successful verification, the backend computed a proof hash and stored it with the accepted ballot record. This proof hash was displayed on the public verification board as part of the voter’s receipt metadata. Early proof-size results were approximately 4,521 to 4,523 bytes for valid binary ballot proofs.

SQLite was used as the database for the prototype. It was selected because it is lightweight, easy to configure, and suitable for a controlled final year implementation. SQLite also supported event-aware tallying by allowing the backend to count accepted ballots linked to the active referendum event. The use of SQLite made the system easier to deploy and test because it did not require a separate managed database service during prototype demonstration.

The database was connected to persistent backend storage during deployment. This was important because ballot and registry records needed to remain available after redeployment. Sensitive data such as voter identity, full NIN, NIN hash, raw vote, decrypted vote, session token, and private proof path were not published on the public board.
4.3.5 Mock NIN Simulation Layer

The mock NIN simulation layer was implemented to model voter accreditation without connecting the prototype to live national identity infrastructure. In the system, a voter submits a mock National Identification Number, which the backend normalises and checks against the controlled mock registry. Only active voters in the registry can proceed to the voting workflow. This layer allows the prototype to demonstrate the principle of eligibility checking while remaining within the ethical and technical scope of a student implementation. It does not connect to the National Identity Management Commission database and does not claim to validate real national identity records.

The mock NIN layer also supports admin-controlled demonstration. Through the admin console, authorised prototype administrators can create, view, deactivate, delete, and reset mock voters. The admin view displays safe identity metadata such as masked NIN and NIN last-four digits, rather than exposing full sensitive identity values. This design supports testing and demonstration while reducing privacy risks. It also keeps the system aligned with the project’s controlled referendum scope.
4.4 Development Methodology

The system was developed using an iterative technical implementation approach. The development process began with requirement identification and system design, followed by implementation of the backend, frontend, database, proof engine, admin console, deployment configuration, and evaluation tests. The implementation was guided by the project objectives, which required the system to review existing e-voting approaches, analyse diaspora voting security requirements, design a zk-STARK-based ballot validity workflow, implement the working prototype, and evaluate its security and performance properties. The development process therefore moved from concept to implementation in stages.

The first implementation stage focused on the backend foundation. This included setting up the Flask API, defining the mock voter registry, implementing login and accreditation logic, creating the event model, and building the voting endpoint. The backend was designed to reject unregistered voters, inactive voters, invalid vote values, unverified sessions, and duplicate voting attempts. This stage established the core server-side rules that controlled ballot access and acceptance.

The second stage focused on the frontend workflow. The React frontend was built to guide users through the voting process. The workflow began with the landing page and continued through mock NIN accreditation, camera-based prototype verification, event selection, ballot selection, review, submission, receipt display, public verification, and tally viewing. This stage was important because a secure voting prototype also needs to be understandable to users. A system that is secure but confusing can still fail in practice, especially in remote voting contexts.

The third stage focused on proof integration. The Winterfell proof engine was connected to the backend vote-submission workflow. The backend generated and verified proof artifacts before storing accepted ballots. Proof hashes were then computed and linked to public ballot receipts. This stage converted the system from a normal voting web application into a proof-backed voting prototype, since ballot acceptance became dependent on proof generation and proof verification.

The fourth stage focused on public verification and tallying. The public board was implemented to display only privacy-preserving receipt metadata. The tally module was implemented to count accepted ballots by event and display Yes, No, total cast, registered voters, and remaining voters where applicable. This stage allowed voters and observers to inspect the public receipt layer and view aggregate results without seeing private ballot choices.

The fifth stage focused on deployment and testing. The backend was deployed on Railway, while the frontend was deployed on Vercel. Environment variables were configured so that the frontend could communicate with the backend and the backend could allow the deployed frontend origin. A Railway volume was used to support persistent backend storage. Smoke testing was then carried out to confirm health checks, voter login, camera verification, vote submission, proof generation, proof verification, public board visibility, tally update, admin operations, and persistence after redeployment.

The deep verifiability upgrade was evaluated with four dedicated scripts and an independent CLI verifier. 4.5.4 Security Analysis

The upgraded security analysis is structured around core verifiability properties rather than only around isolated backend controls. For each property, the report states whether it is achieved, partially achieved, or not achieved, together with the main evidence and the main limitation.

1. Cast-as-intended: partially achieved. Evidence: the voter reviews the binary choice before submission, the backend rejects invalid vote values, and the proof forces the committed vote witness to be binary. Limitation: the prototype does not yet provide an independent voter-side interface for verifying commitment construction before submission, so cast-as-intended assurance still relies partly on the trusted application workflow.

2. Recorded-as-cast: achieved within prototype scope. Evidence: each accepted ballot produces a Ballot ID, nullifier, vote commitment, proof hash, public-board publication, and verification bundle; the CLI verifier can confirm proof validity, proof-hash integrity, receipt consistency, and chain-hash consistency outside Flask. Limitation: the trust model is still single-server and does not yet include a distributed bulletin board.

3. Tallied-as-recorded: achieved within prototype scope. Evidence: tallying is computed from accepted encrypted ballot records, benchmark runs preserved tally correctness at 1,000 backend ballots and in the concurrent stress test, and chain verification confirms that the published board record is internally consistent. Limitation: the tally still depends on backend decryption and does not yet implement a trust-minimised cryptographic tally scheme.

4. Ballot privacy: partially achieved. Evidence: the public board exposes nullifier, vote commitment, proof hash, timestamp, and chain metadata without publishing raw vote values, decrypted votes, full NINs, NIN hashes, salts, private secrets, session tokens, or private proof paths. Limitation: the backend still stores encrypted ballots and performs decryption for tallying, so the design is privacy-preserving but not yet end-to-end secret-ballot perfect in the strongest formal sense.

5. Duplicate-vote prevention: achieved within prototype scope. Evidence: accepted ballots now derive an event-scoped nullifier from a private voter secret and event identifier, the ballot table enforces nullifier uniqueness, duplicate submissions are rejected, and the backend benchmark confirmed nullifier uniqueness correctness. Limitation: the current model still depends on backend-controlled secret derivation rather than a fully decentralised credential system.

6. Public board integrity: achieved within prototype scope. Evidence: every accepted ballot stores previous_chain_hash, current_record_hash, and chain_hash derived from canonical public ballot records; the board verification endpoint recomputes the chain from a fixed genesis hash; the scalability benchmark showed successful chain verification at 1,000 and 10,000 ballots. Limitation: integrity is append-only within one prototype database and is not yet backed by distributed replication or trustee consensus.

7. Independent verifiability: partially achieved. Evidence: the project now exports verification bundles and provides a standalone CLI verifier that runs outside Flask and validates the Winterfell proof, proof hash, receipt consistency, and chain hash. Limitation: a browser/WASM verifier is not yet deployed, and the broader trust model is still smaller than systems such as D-DEMOS that use distributed bulletin boards and stronger formal decentralisation assumptions.
4.5.5 Discussion

The implemented prototype successfully demonstrated the main workflow required by the study. A mock diaspora voter could be accredited, pass camera-based prototype verification, select the active binary referendum, submit a vote, trigger zk-STARK proof generation and verification, receive a public receipt, check the public board, and observe tally updates. This shows that the project was implemented as more than a simple online voting interface. The backend controlled the voting workflow, the proof engine supported proof-backed acceptance, the database stored encrypted ballot records, and the public board provided receipt-based transparency.

The use of a binary referendum was appropriate for the project scope. A full national election with candidates, parties, polling units, wards, local government areas, states, and collation would have introduced unnecessary complexity that could distract from the cryptographic proof objective. The binary referendum allowed the implementation to focus on the essential voting properties: eligibility, duplicate-vote prevention, ballot validity, proof-backed acceptance, public receipt verification, and tally correctness. This made the system testable within the timeframe of a final year project.

The mock NIN layer was also appropriate because it allowed the system to demonstrate voter accreditation without making false claims about live national identity integration. This is important because connecting to real identity systems would require institutional permission, legal agreements, production security controls, and privacy safeguards beyond the scope of the study. The mock layer therefore served as a controlled simulation of the identity-checking role that a real diaspora voting system would require.

The Winterfell proof engine strengthened the prototype by making proof generation and verification part of ballot acceptance. This made the system different from a basic poll application where the server simply stores whatever the frontend submits. However, the implementation also shows that cryptography alone is not enough. The system still needed backend access control, registry checks, event checks, duplicate-vote prevention, encrypted storage, public-board filtering, and tally logic. The most accurate interpretation of the system is therefore a layered trust architecture, where zk-STARK proof verification is one important layer among several.

The evaluation also revealed areas for future improvement. The current public verification model is server-mediated, not fully independent. The camera-based verification step is a prototype presence check, not certified biometric identity matching. The mock NIN registry does not connect to live NIMC infrastructure. The tally is event-aware within the prototype, but the system does not implement national collation or multi-level result aggregation. These limitations do not weaken the project when stated honestly because the objective was to implement a focused, secure diaspora voting prototype rather than a production national voting system.

CHAPTER FIVE: SUMMARY, RECOMMENDATIONS, LIMITATIONS, AND CONCLUSION
5.1 Summary

This study implemented a secure diaspora e-voting prototype for a controlled binary referendum using zk-STARK protocols and then upgraded it for deeper verifiability. The completed system now combines mock voter accreditation, camera-based prototype verification, event-aware ballot handling, proof-backed vote acceptance, encrypted storage, public receipt publication, nullifier-based duplicate-vote prevention, vote commitments, append-only board chaining, and independent verification-bundle export within a single academic workflow.

The project also demonstrated that the trust problem in remote voting is broader than interface design alone. The upgraded prototype shows how backend controls, event checks, binary-vote proof constraints, nullifier derivation, vote commitments, proof hashes, public-board chaining, independent CLI verification, and tally logic can work together as a layered trust architecture. This makes the proof engine materially meaningful rather than merely decorative, while still keeping the scope limited to an academically honest referendum prototype.

From a final year project perspective, the study further demonstrated that a tightly controlled problem definition was necessary to produce an academically defensible implementation. Limiting the ballot model to a binary referendum kept the proof logic, workflow checks, and evaluation evidence aligned with what could be implemented and defended honestly.
5.2 Recommendations
1. The prototype field-friendly hash used inside the Winterfell constraint system should be upgraded to a more standard audited permutation such as Poseidon or Rescue in a future implementation.
2. Stronger identity assurance should be explored only under proper institutional, legal, and privacy approval, especially if future work moves beyond a mock NIN registry.
3. The proof workflow, nullifier derivation, board-chain design, and surrounding backend logic should undergo a formal cryptographic and security audit.

4. Larger-scale performance testing should be carried out with higher ballot volumes, longer safe runtime windows, and stronger hardware so that the already prepared benchmark scripts can be executed at their larger targets.
5. Additional research should address coercion resistance, usability evaluation, and a browser-based or WASM verifier so that independent verification becomes easier for ordinary voters.
6. Deployment hardening and broader trust distribution should be improved before any real-world pilot use is considered, including stronger board replication and clearer external-auditor workflows.

These recommendations are intentionally sequenced around trustworthiness: the first priority is reducing dependence on server-side claims, followed by improving identity assurance, and then stress-testing the combined cryptographic and operational workflow.
5.3 Limitations of the Study
1. The identity layer still uses a mock NIN registry and does not connect to national identity infrastructure.
2. The system still does not integrate with official electoral infrastructure or any official national election backend.
3. The camera-based verification step remains a prototype presence check and not certified biometric identity matching.
4. Independent verification has improved through exported bundles and the standalone CLI verifier, but a browser/WASM verifier is not yet deployed for ordinary voter-side verification.
5. The in-circuit field-friendly hash is a prototype construction and not yet a full production-standard audited voting hash design.
6. The ballot model is still restricted to a controlled binary referendum and does not yet address richer ballot formats.

7. The system does not implement national collation, multi-level aggregation, or polling-unit-to-state result flow, and it still relies on a single-server SQLite trust boundary rather than a distributed bulletin board or trustee network.
8. The prototype is not production-ready for national elections.
5.4 Conclusion

The study achieved its main aim of designing and implementing a secure diaspora e-voting prototype using zk-STARK protocols. More importantly, the upgraded version shows that the proof engine can carry deeper cryptographic meaning by linking public nullifiers and public vote commitments to private witness values while preserving a controlled binary-vote privacy model. Within final year project limits, the prototype now demonstrates cast validation, duplicate-vote resistance, append-only board integrity, and independent verifier support in a technically stronger way than the earlier shallow statement.

Accordingly, the final position of the report is that the prototype is valuable as a proof-of-concept and research instrument, not as a production election platform. Its contribution lies in showing a credible path for combining remote-voting workflow controls with zk-STARK-backed acceptance logic in a Nigerian diaspora-voting context.
